messages.subject: Re: handling escaped untagged animals in capture/trap tables?
messages.subject_clean: handling escaped untagged animals in capture/trap tables?
messages.body_plain:
How many escapes were there? I can't imagine it is really an issue; just omit the records. This will lower the capture rate slightly, but have virtually no effect on density estimates. Your worry about affecting trap availability rather implies we are able to model single-catch traps, but we can't: The standard solution is to treat them as multi-catch traps (always open) which distorts the detection parameter g0 (lambda0), but leaves density estimates unbiased. I think messing with the usage values won't help.

On Friday, November 1, 2019 at 11:34:27 AM UTC+13, Jen Meineke wrote:
> Hello!
>
> I am a MSc student brand new to secr (and still working on learning R) and I have a question about setting up my trap and capture history tables. I am working on small mammals (primarily mice) and I used Sherman traps. I have everything pretty much set, but I don't know how to include information about the mice that happened to escape my technicians during handling before an eartag was placed. I've been researching this problem and I can't seem to find an example of a solution. I don't think I can just omit this data from the dataset, because the traps were closed and thus unavailable for another mouse to be caught, which seems to me like it would impact the trap effort. I had thought about just setting the trap effort for the traps these escapees were caught in as 0.5 (which I am doing for traps that closed without catching anything), but I wasn't sure if this was the appropriate solution or not. Any help would be appreciated and I apologize for the basic question.
>
> Cheers,
>
> Jen

messages.subject: confounding with sex-specific survival in openCR model
messages.subject_clean: confounding with sex-specific survival in openCR model
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I am running an analysis to estimate population growth rate and sex-specific survival to compare the results to estimates derived from a telemetry study of the same population that occurred contemporaneously. Having played around with a lot of variations on detection parameters, I would ideally like to run a JSSAsecrlCL model with sex as a covariate on sigma and phi and a normal movement model, but the variance calculations fail and the error message says confounding likely. When I keep phi constant between sexes, I don't run into any problems. Interestingly, when I run a non-spatial model (p ~ Sex, phi ~ Sex), at least one parameter is not identifiable, but when I run a JSSAsecrlCL model with static movement and sex-specific survival, everything looks good. I have two questions. 1) Is there anything else I can do to try to fit the model with sex-specific survival and activity center movement between sessions (see below for more details)? 2) I know that using static activity centers overestimates sigma and underestimates density, but is there any reason why it would also bias estimates of lambda and phi? Since those are the parameters of interest, should I care about the movement model? The results I get from the static model seem credible.

The dataset isn't great: 269 observations of 54 individuals across 5 sessions. The data come from camera-trap surveys of leopards that occurred in 2005, 2007, 2009, 2011, and 2012. The 2011 survey occurred in a different season and produced very different capture results compared to the other four years. I've attached a simplified script. In addition to the models shown in the script, I played around with starting values, seasonal effects on the fourth session,  kernel radius, and including a finite mixture on move.a, but it hasn't fixed the variance calculations. The kernel radius (20 km) may seem large but has proven necessary for other similar datasets I've been working with.

If anyone does want to take a look at the data, I've posted an rdata file to google drive <https://drive.google.com/open?id=1MjUwjbajAvrwwf1kI26DZNzVUz-4Z8iW> that includes the captures data frame ("captures"), the capthist object ("Ph.ch"), a mask object ("msk"), a non-spatial model ("CRmod"), an openCR_list of four spatial models with a "normal" movement model ("openSCR_list"), and a spatial model with a static movement model ("static_mod").

Any suggestions or insights would be greatly appreciated.

Matt Rogan

messages.subject_clean: Slightly different results when running the same data/model in new version 4.0.2
messages.body_plain:
I updated secr to v4.0.2 and am observing some differences in results from the same model/data inputs under version 3.1.2. For the half normal, hazard rate, and binary signal strength detection functions, the results differ only slightly. However, for the compound half normal or cumulative log normal detection functions, the results are very different. This only seems to happen with multiple sessions. Running single session inputs gives identical results across versions. Is this to be expected with the major rewrite for v4? I didn't see any mention of differences for multiple sessions in the documentation, but wanted to check to try and understand what is going on.

I am working with acoustic data and binary detection/no detection capture histories across multiple recorders.

Two examples:

Only slight differences
Ran with version 3.1.2
res.hn.multiSess<-secr.fit(capthist,detectfn=0,start=c(log(50),qnorm(0.8),log(20)),mask=mask,verify=FALSE,trace=FALSE)

        link   estimate  SE.estimate        lcl        ucl
D       log  7.9974215 1.816525e+00  5.1527067 12.4126512
g0    logit  0.9999999 2.873903e-16  0.9999999  0.9999999
sigma   log 21.3430790 2.309188e+00 17.2754821 26.3684116

Ran with version 4.0.2
res.hn.multiSess<-secr.fit(capthist,detectfn=0,start=c(log(50),qnorm(0.8),log(20)),mask=mask,details = list(fastproximity = FALSE), verify=FALSE,trace=FALSE)

       link   estimate  SE.estimate        lcl        ucl
D       log  7.4340499 1.700976e+00  4.7746588 11.5746694
g0    logit  0.9999999 8.039165e-15  0.9999999  0.9999999
sigma   log 22.2879969 2.413045e+00 18.0377643 27.5397104

Major differences
Ran with version 3.1.2
res_chn_allSesh = secr.fit(captHistAllSesh, CL = TRUE, detectfn=3, start=c(qnorm(0.9),log(600), log(40)), mask = make.mask(trapsAllSeshList,buffer = 8000), verify = FALSE)
       link  estimate  SE.estimate        lcl        ucl
g0    logit   1.00000 3.835994e-17   1.000000    1.00000
sigma   log 957.75105 1.003033e+02 780.460672 1175.31492
z       log  11.24813 4.777312e+00   5.063356   24.98745

Ran with version 4.0.2
res_chn_allSesh = secr.fit(captHistAllSesh, CL = TRUE, detectfn=3, start=c(qnorm(0.9),log(600), log(40)), mask = make.mask(trapsAllSeshList,buffer = 8000), details = list(fastproximity = FALSE), verify = FALSE)
       link     estimate SE.estimate           lcl           ucl
g0    logit 5.907125e-03   0.9156145 1.127831e-135  1.000000e+00
sigma   log 9.434526e+02  98.2626056  7.696702e+02  1.156473e+03
z       log 2.187084e+03         Inf 1.621558e-129 2.949839e+135

Hello Selene
I can't give a definite answer, but in each case one of the parameters is being estimated at a boundary or is unidentifiable, and erratic results aren't too surprising. It would be illuminating to fix the offending parameter (e.g. fixed = list(g0=1.0)) and see if the remaining estimates are consistent between versions. I can't think of an explanation specific to multi-session data.
Murray

messages.subject: Home Range Size using circular.r
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am wanting to make sure that I am calculating home range radius and size properly. I have found one or two posts here about calculating 95% home range using circular.r, like this:

radius <- circular.r(detectfn = "HEX", detectpar = list(sigma = sig))

My searches on here for calculating home range from this radius have led me to a few different options, so I am not entirely clear on what formula to use. What I've found is

HR95 <- (pi*(3.36*sig)^2)

What is the correct formula for calculating 95% home range from the circular.r radius? I am using the "HEX" detection function.

Thank you
